definition: Expiate means to make amends for a wrong.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word expiate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know expiate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Decades after the false expulsion, the old headmaster tried to expiate his injustice by endowing a scholarship in the wronged student's name.
An apology costs one sentence and a moment's humility; apologize stops far short of expiate, which pays for the wrong with real acts over time.
To repent is to feel the wrong sincerely and turn from it; repent stops short of expiate, which goes on to settle the debt in deeds.

To redeem is to buy back your good name, sometimes with a single shining act that restores you to favor. Expiate stays fixed on the wrong itself: you pay the moral debt down, act by act, until the account is settled. Redeem rescues the person; expiate settles the offense.

To atone is the general word for making amends — you atone for a wrong, and a change of heart alone can count. Expiate leans harder on the outward payment: the labor, cost, or gift that settles the account. You expiate a wrong; the person you injured is never its object.

And note its object — you expiate a wrong, a sin, or guilt itself, not the person you injured.
Expiate keeps company with sin, guilt, and old wrongs — sermons and novels more than newsrooms.

The shipowner Josiah Brant made his fortune the way many did in the 1860s: by loading his freighters until the waterline vanished.
When the overloaded Meridian went down with nineteen hands, an inquiry faulted the practice but fined him barely a week's profit.
The law was finished with Brant; by every account, Brant was not finished with himself.
Over the next thirty years he paid for eleven lifeboat stations along the coast, one for each year of his overloading, and required each to log the crews it saved.
He called the ledger his debt-book, and those who knew him said he was not giving charity but working to expiate a wrong -- settling, entry by entry, an account only he still kept.
